data.title: Cochin Shipyard's (NSE:COCHINSHIP) Sluggish Earnings Might Be Just The Beginning Of Its Problems
data.description:
Last week's earnings announcement from Cochin Shipyard Limited (NSE:COCHINSHIP) was disappointing to investors, with a sluggish profit figure. We did some analysis, and found that there are some reasons to be cautious about the headline numbers.

Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.

A Closer Look At Cochin Shipyard's Earnings

One key financial ratio used to measure how well a company converts its profit to free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. You could think of the accrual ratio from cashflow as the 'non-FCF profit ratio'.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

Over the twelve months to September 2026, Cochin Shipyard recorded an accrual ratio of 0.37. As a general rule, that bodes poorly for future profitability. To wit, the company did not generate one whit of free cashflow in that time. In the last twelve months it actually had negative free cash flow, with an outflow of ₹11b despite its profit of ₹6.27b, mentioned above. Coming off the back of negative free cash flow last year, we imagine some shareholders might wonder if its cash burn of ₹11b, this year, indicates high risk.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On Cochin Shipyard's Profit Performance

As we have made quite clear, we're a bit worried that Cochin Shipyard didn't back up the last year's profit with free cashflow. As a result, we think it may well be the case that Cochin Shipyard's underlying earnings power is lower than its statutory profit. Nonetheless, it's still worth noting that its earnings per share have grown at 46% over the last three years. The goal of this article has been to assess how well we can rely on the statutory earnings to reflect the company's potential, but there is plenty more to consider. data.title: Elecom's (TSE:6750) Attractive Earnings Are Not All Good News For Shareholders
data.description:
Even though Elecom Co., Ltd. (TSE:6750) posted strong earnings recently, the stock hasn't reacted in a large way. We looked deeper into the numbers and found that shareholders might be concerned with some underlying weaknesses.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Zooming In On Elecom's Earnings

In high finance, the key ratio used to measure how well a company converts reported profits into free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio (from cashflow). The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

For the year to September 2026, Elecom had an accrual ratio of 0.41. Ergo, its free cash flow is significantly weaker than its profit. As a general rule, that bodes poorly for future profitability. Indeed, in the last twelve months it reported free cash flow of JP¥6.2b, which is significantly less than its profit of JP¥21.4b. Elecom's free cash flow actually declined over the last year, but it may bounce back next year, since free cash flow is often more volatile than accounting profits. However, that's not the end of the story. We must also consider the impact of unusual items on statutory profit (and thus the accrual ratio), as well as note the ramifications of the company issuing new shares. The good news for shareholders is that Elecom's accrual ratio was much better last year, so this year's poor reading might simply be a case of a short term mismatch between profit and FCF. Shareholders should look for improved cashflow relative to profit in the current year, if that is indeed the case.

View our latest analysis for Elecom

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

One essential aspect of assessing earnings quality is to look at how much a company is diluting shareholders. As it happens, Elecom issued 5.5% more new shares over the last year. Therefore, each share now receives a smaller portion of profit. Per share metrics like EPS help us understand how much actual shareholders are benefitting from the company's profits, while the net income level gives us a better view of the company's absolute size. Check out Elecom's historical EPS growth by clicking on this link.

A Look At The Impact Of Elecom's Dilution On Its Earnings Per Share (EPS)

As you can see above, Elecom has been growing its net income over the last few years, with an annualized gain of 158% over three years. And the 110% profit boost in the last year certainly seems impressive at first glance. But in comparison, EPS only increased by 101% over the same period. And so, you can see quite clearly that dilution is influencing shareholder earnings.

In the long term, earnings per share growth should beget share price growth. So Elecom shareholders will want to see that EPS figure continue to increase. However, if its profit increases while its earnings per share stay flat (or even fall) then shareholders might not see much benefit. For the ordinary retail shareholder, EPS is a great measure to check your hypothetical "share" of the company's profit.

The Impact Of Unusual Items On Profit

The fact that the company had unusual items boosting profit by JP¥8.2b, in the last year, probably goes some way to explain why its accrual ratio was so weak. While we like to see profit increases, we tend to be a little more cautious when unusual items have made a big contribution. When we analysed the vast majority of listed companies worldwide, we found that significant unusual items are often not repeated. And that's as you'd expect, given these boosts are described as 'unusual'. We can see that Elecom's positive unusual items were quite significant relative to its profit in the year to September 2026. As a result, we can surmise that the unusual items are making its statutory profit significantly stronger than it would otherwise be.

Our Take On Elecom's Profit Performance

Elecom didn't back up its earnings with free cashflow, but this isn't too surprising given profits were inflated by unusual items. Meanwhile, the new shares issued mean that shareholders now own less of the company, unless they tipped in more cash themselves. For all the reasons mentioned above, we think that, at a glance, Elecom's statutory profits could be considered to be low quality, because they are likely to give investors an overly positive impression of the company. With this in mind, we wouldn't consider investing in a stock unless we had a thorough understanding of the risks. The Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation Limited (NSE:BBTC) just reported healthy earnings but the stock price didn't move much. Investors are probably missing some underlying factors which are encouraging for the future of the company.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Zooming In On Bombay Burmah Trading's Earnings

One key financial ratio used to measure how well a company converts its profit to free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

For the year to September 2026, Bombay Burmah Trading had an accrual ratio of -0.16. Therefore, its statutory earnings were very significantly less than its free cashflow. To wit, it produced free cash flow of ₹28b during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of ₹13.0b. Bombay Burmah Trading shareholders are no doubt pleased that free cash flow improved over the last twelve months.

Our Take On Bombay Burmah Trading's Profit Performance

As we discussed above, Bombay Burmah Trading has perfectly satisfactory free cash flow relative to profit. Based on this observation, we consider it likely that Bombay Burmah Trading's statutory profit actually understates its earnings potential! And the EPS is up 15% over the last twelve months. Of course, we've only just scratched the surface when it comes to analysing its earnings; one could also consider margins, forecast growth, and return on investment, among other factors. While earnings are important, another area to consider is the balance sheet. We've done some analysis and you can see our take on Bombay Burmah Trading's balance sheet by clicking here.

This note has only looked at a single factor that sheds light on the nature of Bombay Burmah Trading's profit. But there is always more to discover if you are capable of focussing your mind on minutiae. data.description:
Record US energy exports highlight how critical reliable power infrastructure has become for governments and households that need stable electricity, not just cheap fossil fuels. For Australian investors, dependable fully franked dividend payers tied to essential services can turn that same theme into steady cash flow. This piece walks through three high quality ASX dividend stocks that aim to convert durable earnings into tax effective income.

The three dividend ideas in this piece are just a sample, with the full screen surfacing 17 more fully franked income plays that carry equally detailed narratives not covered below. To identify your own mix of dependable payers built for SMSFs and income-first portfolios, head straight into the Best ASX Fully Franked Dividend Shares screener

Nick Scali (ASX:NCK)

Overview: Nick Scali is a long-established furniture retailer that uses its showrooms and online channels to turn sofa and homeware sales into cash for fully franked dividends.

Operations: The group generates A$516.7 million from furniture retailing, with about A$476.7 million in Australia and New Zealand and A$40 million in the United Kingdom.

Market Cap: A$1.1 billion

Nick Scali matters for the Best ASX Fully Franked Dividend Shares screener because its furniture retail cash flows are closely aligned with dividend capacity, and the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St sets out how current expansion plans and capital backing could shape that income profile over time.

"The UK turnaround plan, including completion of refurbishments across 16 stores, rebranding to Nick Scali, alignment of product with Australia and a move into a leased warehouse, has already lifted gross margin to just above 60% and is expected to improve group profitability as written orders scale towards the lower breakeven revenue level."

For income-focused investors, what happens if one unseen pressure on those margins and cash flows moves in the wrong direction will matter a lot.

Those unseen pressures are exactly where the full narrative for Nick Scali digs in, showing where Nick Scali’s dividend story could accelerate or stall as conditions shift.

Super Retail Group (ASX:SUL)

Overview: Super Retail Group runs the Supercheap Auto, rebel, BCF and Macpac chains, turning everyday auto, sports and outdoor spending into cash-generative retail earnings that support fully franked dividends.

Operations: The group generates about A$1.6 billion from Supercheap Auto, A$1.4 billion from rebel, A$953 million from BCF and A$240 million from Macpac across Australia and New Zealand.

Market Cap: A$2.9 billion

Super Retail Group matters to this fully franked income screen because, according to Sax, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the Narrative, its auto and outdoor chains convert regular consumer spending into the kind of repeatable cash flow SMSFs look for in franked payouts.

"Another significant risk is elevated interest rates and cost-of-living pressures which constrain discretionary spending, adversely impacting SUL’s revenue and potentially necessitating lower dividend payouts."

What happens if a quiet shift in how shoppers prioritise car care and outdoor gear spending breaks the current earnings rhythm will really count.

That quiet shift is exactly what the full narrative for Super Retail Group unpacks, revealing where Super Retail Group’s cash generation could quietly accelerate even if headline spending looks stalled.

Evolution Mining (ASX:EVN)

Overview: Evolution Mining runs gold and gold copper mines in Australia and Canada, turning production from assets like Cowal and Mungari into cash flow.

Operations: Evolution Mining generates about A$1.8b from Cowal, A$1.0b from Mungari, A$1.0b from Ernest Henry, A$806 million from Red Lake, A$616 million from Northparkes and smaller amounts from Mt Rawdon and corporate activities.

Market Cap: A$21.4b

Evolution Mining matters for this fully franked dividend screen because its gold and copper cash flows underpin franked payouts. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St describes how that mine portfolio could shape future income strength.

"Growing copper exposure through operations such as Ernest Henry and Northparkes, where copper currently contributes about 22% of Evolution Mining revenue and benefits from low C1 cost positions and latent processing capacity, is expected to influence future revenue mix and unit margins."

What happens if one unseen pressure on those cost positions and capital needs moves the wrong way will heavily influence dividend reliability.
